blurb: Natural island cat of the Greek Cyclades, mostly white and fond of water
description: The Aegean cat is a natural landrace from Greece's Cycladic Islands: medium-sized, muscular and semi-longhaired, usually bicolor with white, lively and social.
answer: The Aegean is a naturally occurring landrace of domestic cat from the Cycladic Islands of Greece and western Turkey, considered the only native Greek cat variety. It is a medium-sized, muscular, semi-longhaired cat, usually bicolor or tricolor with white, and is described as intelligent, active and communicative.

body: Aegean cats developed through natural selection on the Cycladic Islands, where cats are thought to have been introduced during the Bronze Age, making them one of the oldest domesticated varieties. They are common as feral cats around the fishing ports of Greece and Turkey, are considered a national treasure in Greece, and are notable predators of Aegean wall lizards.
Greek breeders began selective breeding to develop a formal breed in the early 1990s, but the Aegean has not yet been recognized by any major cat registry.

The Aegean is a medium-sized, muscular, semi-longhaired cat with medium round paws, a tail that can be long and 'hooked', and wide-based ears with rounded, furred tips. Eyes are almond-shaped and may be any shade of green, blue or yellow.
The coat is bicolor or tricolor, almost always including white, which usually covers 25% to 90% of the body; the other colors and patterns vary widely.

Having lived alongside people for centuries, the Aegean is described as well adapted to humans: a social, intelligent, active and lively cat that communicates readily and does not hesitate to seek attention. It is noted for an affinity for water and fishing.
Sources give little detailed care advice, but the Aegean is said to tolerate apartment living rather well. As an active, lively cat it will likely appreciate play and attention.

Because the Aegean developed through natural selection rather than selective breeding, it is described as free from most feline genetic diseases. The sources name no specific conditions; regular veterinary check-ups are recommended.
